analysis.one_liner: Requires groups spending on elections to reveal their big donors and tightens the ban on foreign money.
analysis.headline: The DISCLOSE Act of 2023 never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate Rules Committee, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force corporations, unions, super PACs, and tax-exempt "dark money" groups to report any election-related spending over $10,000 to the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours, and to identify the individuals who ultimately control them. Political ads would have to name an organization's top five funders on screen, and it would become a federal crime carrying up to five years in prison to set up a company to hide foreign money in elections. The bill also extends the existing foreign-money ban to digital ads, ballot initiative campaigns, and spending on Supreme Court and other judicial nominations.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would learn who is actually paying for the political ads and robocalls they see — including which corporations, wealthy individuals, or foreign-linked entities are behind groups that currently hide their funders. The bill also helps election enforcers, by giving the FEC new tools and FinCEN data to catch foreign money and by requiring a government audit of illicit foreign spending each presidential cycle.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters seeking to know who funds ads

how_it_helps.text: Any corporation, union, tax-exempt group, or super PAC spending more than $10,000 on elections would have to file a report with the FEC within 24 hours, listing its beneficial owners and naming anyone who gave it $10,000 or more.

Political ads would have to show a 'Top Five Funders' list of the donors who gave the sponsoring organization the most money in the past year, and the CEO or top official would have to personally state the group 'approves this message.'
Setting up or using a company to conceal a foreign national's election contribution would become a crime punishable by up to five years in prison and a fine.

The foreign-money ban would be extended to paid web and digital ads, ballot initiatives and referenda, and spending on federal judicial nominations, with a GAO study of illicit foreign money required for each four-year election cycle.

analysis.who_pays: Dark money groups, super PACs, corporations, and labor unions that spend on elections would lose the ability to spend anonymously: they would face new reporting, perjury-backed certifications, and ads carrying their top funders' names. Large digital platforms and advertisers would bear new disclaimer duties on political ads. Spenders who want the public not to know who is behind their messaging are the ones with something to lose.
analysis.who_pays_short: Dark money groups and big spenders

drawbacks.text: Disclosure requirements can expose donors to public criticism, boycotts, or harassment; the bill acknowledges this and carves out an exception allowing donors to withhold their names if they would face serious threats, harassment, or reprisals.

Covered organizations — including nonprofits and business leagues, not just political committees — would face substantial new compliance duties, including beneficial-ownership reports and perjury-backed certifications from their top executives, and critics argue these burdens can deter lawful participation in politics.

Opponents of disclosure laws have argued they burden political speech, even though the bill's own findings cite Supreme Court language that disclosure is a 'less restrictive alternative' to direct spending limits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is information: voters currently see ads from groups that are legally allowed to keep their funders secret, and this bill would attach names to the money. The main costs are compliance burdens on thousands of organizations and a real, though partly addressed, risk of donor harassment. Because the Supreme Court has repeatedly called disclosure the least restrictive form of campaign regulation — language the bill itself quotes — the tradeoff weighs toward disclosure, though the 24-hour reporting cadence and broad definition of covered transfers would be genuinely demanding for smaller organizations.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill and sent it to its Rules and Administration Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the DISCLOSE Act on February 16, 2023, with 50 Senate colleagues signing on as cosponsors — 48 Democrats and 3 independents, including Majority Leader Chuck Schumer.
The bill's only action after introduction was to be read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration.
The committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor during the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.
Every cosponsor was a Democrat or independent; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced to a vote where senators would have had to cast a public record on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Groups and donors who spend money to influence elections anonymously kept that ability untouched. No organization spending dark money in 2024 elections had to reveal its funders, and the loopholes allowing foreign-linked money into ballot measure campaigns and digital ads remain open.

sides.party_line_note: All 51 cosponsors were Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats, and no Republican sponsored the bill; campaign finance disclosure has split almost entirely on party lines in recent Congresses.

industries.note: These groups spent an estimated $1.05 billion in the 2020 cycle without naming donors; the bill would require them to report spending over $10,000 within 24 hours and identify their beneficial owners and top funders. Their interest in continued anonymity runs directly against voters' interest in knowing who pays for political messages.

industries.industry: Super PACs and large political spenders
industries.note: Spending over $10,000 would trigger rapid disclosure of the sources of their money, ending the ability to route funds through intermediaries to mask original donors. Wealthy donors giving $10,000 or more would appear by name in public filings.

industries.industry: Corporations and labor unions making political expenditures
industries.note: Both are 'covered organizations' subject to the new reporting and disclaimer rules, though the bill includes special attribution rules for dues-funded union transfers and exempts ordinary commercial receipts. Neither would be banned from spending — only required to say who is paying.

industries.industry: Large digital platforms and political ad buyers
industries.note: Platforms with 50 million or more monthly U.S. users would face new disclaimer and top-funder display requirements on paid political ads, adding compliance work. The rules increase transparency for the public at the cost of some friction for ad operations.

The bill criminalizes using shell companies to hide foreign election money and extends the foreign-money ban to digital ads and ballot initiatives, with up to five years in prison. This is an enforcement gain for election integrity that the public generally supports across party lines.
